View:
A node-link graph of subject places that co-occur in the same record (the same relationship the "subject place ↔ subject place" links describe). Node size = records here; fill color = detected community; ring thickness/brightness = coreness (how deeply embedded in a mutually-reinforcing cluster -- thick/bright = core, thin/dark = periphery). Building network…
What are modularity & communities?
A "community" here is a cluster of places that co-occur with each other (as subjects of the same records) noticeably more than they co-occur with the rest of the network — found by greedy modularity optimization (the core step of the Louvain method), not assigned by hand. "Modularity" (Q) scores the whole partition from -0.5 to 1: how much more internal linkage the found clusters have than you'd expect from a random network with the same node degrees. Above ~0.3 usually means real structure, not noise -- though one dominant hub community (like a "Ukraine" cluster in a Ukraine-history collection) mathematically drags the score down even when the partition is meaningful, since a hub's own contribution can go slightly negative. Click a community below to isolate it.
What's core vs. periphery?
This is an ego/degeneracy view of the same graph, independent of the community split above. Each place's "coreness" (k-core number) is the deepest peeling round it survives: strip away whatever currently has only 1 connection, then whatever now has only 2, and so on -- coreness is the round a place finally falls out at. High coreness = sits inside a densely, mutually-reinforcing cluster (the network's structural "core"); coreness 0-1 = hangs off by a single link with nothing backing it up ("periphery"). Pin any place (click it on the map or in the network) to see its own ego-network stats in the right panel: how many places it connects to, its coreness, which community it's in, and how interconnected ITS neighbors are with each other.
What's a "structural bridge"?
Also independent of the community split. A place's betweenness score asks: across every pair of OTHER places, how often does the shortest path between them run through here? A place with modest degree can still score high if its few connections happen to stitch together parts of the network that would otherwise only route through the dominant hub -- removing it would fragment the graph more than its connection count suggests. The single biggest hub (if there is one) usually tops the list trivially, since almost every path runs through it; the more telling entries are further down, where degree is low but the bridge score isn't.

Temporal aboutness — what places are written ABOUT

These records' subject headings never name a place with a date (often because they're about a PERSON or ORGANIZATION — a biography or bibliography — rather than a place), so there's nothing to plot on this layer at ANY date range. They're not missing from the collection, just from this particular view.
Year of publication — where books were PUBLISHED
Scale is compressed before the dashed line (1980) — nearly 95% of dated records were published after that, so recent decades get more room to work with.

Off by default: the two timelines are independent (a record can be ABOUT the 1930s and PUBLISHED in 2015). Turn this on to require both — e.g. only records ABOUT your selected years that were ALSO published in your selected years.
For each currently-shown record, draws an arc from where it was PUBLISHED to what place it is ABOUT. Thicker/brighter arcs = more records share that pair. Hover an arc for details.
For each currently-shown record that's ABOUT two or more places at once, draws an arc between every pair of those places. Thicker/brighter arcs = more records mention that pair together. Hover an arc for details.
